title: Build your first AI agent
quote:
One canteen. Two tools.
Your first agent.
bottom: Vedant · VIT Mumbai · 17 October 2026
say: We will build a small program that uses AI to choose tools. By the end you should understand one working loop and know why you might choose a graph or a team.
do: Have the new learner folder ready, with no menu_tools.py or my_agent.py. Open only the lesson and clean terminal; close private .env tabs.
ask: Who has used a chatbot? Who has written a Python function?
fallback: Sharing and checkpoint files are available. Do not turn the introduction into installation support.

title: You have Rs 80 and ten minutes
quote:
Find vegetarian lunch.
Is the canteen still open?
bottom: What information would the program need?
say: Use a familiar deadline: the next lecture starts soon and you need lunch. Ask what information matters before saying any framework names.
do: Show a rehearsed short real run if available. Otherwise state clearly that the scripted preview is a rehearsal and the actual tool data is local.
ask: Budget? Diet? Availability? Opening hours?
fallback: Use classroom/saved_runs/agent.txt. Read its SCRIPTED label aloud.

title: What makes this an agent?
rows: Use a menu or hours lookup.
bottom: An AI program can choose steps and use tools toward a goal.
say: The agent is the whole program: model, instructions, permitted tools and the loop around them. A model response alone is not Python execution.
ask: Does the model magically know our current menu?

title: Act out the tool call
bottom: The model requests. Application code executes.
say: Ask three volunteers to play the user, model and menu tool. Keep the whole role-play to two minutes. The tool holder has the four fictional records. The model must ask for them before recommending food.
do: Use the menu on the next slide or the data file; no printed props are required.
ask: Who actually looked at the menu?
fallback: Play all three roles from the front if volunteers are slow.

title: Give each part one job
bottom: Tool result returns to the model, which continues or finishes.
say: Name each part only after the role-play. Point from user to model to application function, and then back with the result. Do not add MCP or multi-agent terminology yet.
ask: Can the model request a function our app has not allowed?

title: Our entire canteen menu
bottom: Predict the answer for a vegetarian budget of Rs 80.
say: Four records are enough. Only the sandwich qualifies. The hours fixture is 09:00-16:00 and mock time is 12:30. These are fictional teaching records.
do: Switch briefly to classroom/data/menu.json and point out the four fields. Return to the slide before typing.
ask: Why does the cheaper poha not qualify?

title: A tool starts as a function
bottom: This outline is ordinary Python. Complete it in the editor.
say: Explain function, argument and return value just in time. This slide is an outline with an ellipsis, not the runnable solution. Use the full small function in the lesson.
do: In your new learner folder create menu_tools.py. Add imports/data loading, then find_food from classroom/README.md. Use the readable for loop. Run: & $py menu_tools.py
ask: Which values go in? What comes back?
fallback: Open classroom/menu_tools.py as the labelled completed checkpoint.

title: Your turn: run the tool
quote:
Create menu_tools.py
Call find_food(80)
Then try find_food(30)
bottom: Checkpoint 1: a real local function result
say: Give students three minutes to run it. Show the slide while they type. Ask for ready/help/checkpoint signals. Do not inspect every laptop.
do: Expect sandwich at 80 and an empty matches list at 30. Remove the temporary top-level print before importing the module.
ask: Is an empty result the same as a failed lookup?
fallback: Copy classroom/menu_tools.py into the learner folder, or read its saved result and label what happened.

title: Let the model request the function
bottom: The application executes the requested function.
say: The description tells the model when the function is relevant. A tool request has a name and arguments. The library routes an allowed request to Python and returns the actual result.
do: Point to the name find_food and max_price=80 in a saved or rehearsed live trace.
ask: Who reads the JSON file?

title: The ReAct-style loop
bottom: Continue, use another tool, or finish within a limit.
say: Explain ReAct as reasoning and acting in a loop. We inspect tool actions and results, not private chain-of-thought. Our tool-calling agent illustrates this pattern; we are not reproducing every detail of the original paper.
do: Explain the five-line conceptual loop in the preparation guide. LangChain manages message bookkeeping in the student build.
ask: What should happen when the agent has enough information?

title: Build with LangChain
code:
agent = create_agent(
    model=make_model(OFFLINE),
    tools=[tool(find_food)],
    system_prompt="Use the menu for facts.",
)
result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [("user", "Veg lunch under Rs 80?")]},
    {"recursion_limit": 10},
)
bottom: Add imports and setup from classroom/README.md.
say: Write this in a new my_agent.py. Explain model, tools and instruction. make_model is supplied configuration/fallback support; create_agent is the framework loop. OFFLINE=True is scripted rehearsal; False requires a privately configured tested live model.
do: Use the full 18-line first-agent checkpoint from classroom/README.md. Add imports, then agent creation, then invocation and show_messages. Run: & $py my_agent.py
ask: Where did we give the model permission to request find_food?
fallback: Use classroom/first_agent_checkpoint.py after the menu tool exists.

title: Build and run your first agent
quote:
Write my_agent.py
Register your menu function
Ask for lunch under Rs 80
bottom: Checkpoint 2: explain one tool request and its result
say: Protect these ten minutes. Let students type and run the small file. Stay on this slide. Volunteers handle individual setup; explain repeated mistakes from the front.
do: Use & $py my_agent.py in the learner folder. Have students point to MODEL REQUEST and RESULT. Explain the mode label. For live calls, observe actual behavior rather than expecting an exact sentence.
ask: What did you write, and what did LangChain handle?
fallback: Run & $py classroom/agent.py --offline from repository root, or use the saved output. Label checkpoint use accurately.

title: What happened in that run?
rows: find_food with a budget and diet
Python reads and filters our menu
The model receives the actual result
bottom: Try a different question and observe the tool use.
say: Give about two minutes for a budget/question variation and three minutes for discussion. Explain what repeats and what finishes. A normal model can choose a different order or not need a tool for a greeting.
do: Try Rs 30. Distinguish an empty successful result from an error, without opening the advanced error-handling lab.
ask: Could it answer opening hours with only this tool?

title: Add one new ability
code:
def get_canteen_hours(at: str = "12:30") -> dict:
    """Read fictional hours at a mock time."""
    # See the full short function in the lesson.
    ...

tools=[tool(find_food), tool(get_canteen_hours)]
bottom: Registering a new tool gives the agent another allowed action.
say: Write the full hours function from the lesson. This slide is an outline. We use a mock clock so everyone can reproduce the same case; it is not live campus data.
do: Add hours to menu_tools.py, update the import and tools list in my_agent.py. Show only these changes.
ask: What should we ask so the program needs both tools?

title: Your agent now has two tools
quote:
Find vegetarian lunch under Rs 80
and tell me when the canteen closes
bottom: Checkpoint 3: run the capability you added
say: Give students seven minutes. In a real model run the tool order may vary; what matters is that menu/hours claims have the relevant results. Scripted rehearsal follows a known sequence.
do: Run my_agent.py again. Expect sandwich and mock closing 16:00. Take two short student explanations from different seating zones.
ask: Which part did you add? Which question now works?
fallback: The completed classroom/agent.py is the two-tool checkpoint.

title: Five-minute break
quote:
Back at 12:00
Keep your first agent open
bottom: Next: reuse its tools through MCP
say: Stop for the full five-minute break. Let volunteers help setup during the pause without making it another lecture.
do: Resume at 12:00. Bring up the MCP question, not installation steps.

title: Can another app use our tools?
quote:
We already wrote the menu logic.
How can another agent reuse it?
bottom: MCP gives applications a common tool interface.
say: Motivate the boundary after the function works. A common MCP server exposes tools; it does not provide a model or make the system autonomous.
ask: What would be wasteful about rewriting the menu filter for every framework?

title: Same data, same tool service
rows: The same fictional menu and clock
bottom: Framework connections differ. The tool contract stays the same.
say: Each example starts a local stdio instance of the same server program. We are not deploying a central campus server. The functions remain ordinary Python.
do: Point to menu_tools.py being imported by mcp_server.py.
ask: Does MCP replace the model?

title: Expose our functions through MCP
code:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
from menu_tools import find_food, get_canteen_hours

server = FastMCP("Campus Canteen")
server.tool()(find_food)
server.tool()(get_canteen_hours)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run(transport="stdio")
bottom: Use the same functions. Keep server stdout for protocol traffic.
say: Write mcp_server.py. Explain registration as making the functions discoverable to a client. No need to teach async internals or every transport.
do: Create the file in the learner folder. The supplied connection helper launches it through the current Python interpreter; no separate server window is needed.

title: Discover, call, then connect an agent
code:
async with connected_tools() as tools:
    print([t.name for t in tools])
    # The client has real MCP tool wrappers.
    agent = create_agent(make_model(OFFLINE), tools)
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [("user", "Veg lunch under Rs 80?")]}
    )
bottom: Prepared connection setup lets us focus on the tool boundary.
say: First list tools and call find_food directly through MCP; that does not need a model. Then show classroom/mcp_agent.py. connected_tools owns a local connection and closes it after use.
do: From repository root: & $py classroom/mcp_probe.py, then & $py classroom/mcp_agent.py --offline. Remove --offline only for a privately rehearsed live run.
ask: Which part moved into another process?

title: Try one real MCP call
quote:
Discover the two tools
Call find_food with budget 80
Compare with your direct function
bottom: Checkpoint 4: same records across a process boundary
say: Give students three and a half minutes for the probe from the lesson where setup permits. The local MCP call is real even without an LLM key.
do: Run probe.py in the learner folder, or use classroom/mcp_probe.py from repository root. See the two tool names and sandwich result.
ask: What stayed the same?
fallback: Keep the direct-function agent and watch the instructor MCP call; complete local setup after class.

title: What if the canteen is closed?
quote:
We want to check hours first.
If closed, skip the lunch lookup.
bottom: Now we have a reason to control the route.
say: Use a concrete requirement before introducing graph vocabulary. The earlier agent chooses tools; this outer workflow guarantees an hours step first.
ask: Would a menu lookup help when the canteen is closed?

title: One branch around an agent
code:
START -> check hours

    open   -> lunch agent -> END
    closed -> closed reply -> END

State = information carried forward
Node  = one step
Edge  = the next route
bottom: LangGraph can combine explicit steps and flexible agent loops.
say: Read the route together. State holds hours, question and answer. A node is an ordinary function that updates that information. An edge chooses the next step. The open node contains the familiar agent.
ask: Where does the model choose its own actions here?

title: Wire the small graph
code:
flow = StateGraph(State)
flow.add_node("hours", hours)
flow.add_node("agent", agent)
flow.add_node("closed", closed)
flow.add_edge(START, "hours")
flow.add_conditional_edges(
    "hours", choose, {"agent": "agent", "closed": "closed"}
)
flow.add_edge("agent", END)
flow.add_edge("closed", END)
bottom: The graph file defines three steps and one branch.
say: This is an instructor demonstration. Students can read the three functions and wiring. Do not require the room to type the whole graph.
do: Open classroom/graph.py. Point to hours using MCP and agent containing create_agent. Explain choose without adding persistence or approval APIs.

title: Predict both routes, then run
code:
python classroom/graph.py --offline

# Simulated later time:
python classroom/graph.py --offline --at 17:00

12:30 -> hours -> agent
17:00 -> hours -> closed
bottom: The closed route skips the lunch agent.
say: Ask for predictions before each run. Both calls use the same actual MCP server. The offline brain is scripted. The closed route does not invoke the lunch agent.
do: Use & $py rather than python if using the prepared PowerShell interpreter variable.
ask: What would you change to add an approval step later?

title: Could two agents share the job?
bottom: One role gathers facts. The next uses those facts.
say: Use a group lunch for two vegetarians within Rs 150. Scout gathers options under Rs 75 per person. Planner proposes quantities and a total. This is a deliberately small example of a handoff, not proof that two agents improve lunch search.
ask: Could one agent already do this?

title: A real CrewAI handoff
code:
lookup = Task(..., agent=scout)
plan = Task(..., agent=planner, context=[lookup])

team = Crew(
    agents=[scout, planner],
    tasks=[lookup, plan],
    process=Process.sequential,
)
team.kickoff()
bottom: context passes the first task output into the next task.
say: This excerpt is an outline; open the runnable file. Show Agent, Task and Crew objects. Only the scout has the menu tool, discovered through the same MCP program. This is sequential, not a manager dynamically choosing workers.
do: Open classroom/crew.py. The presenter has already installed requirements-instructor.txt. Keep adapter compatibility details out of the beginner explanation.

title: Run the scout and planner
code:
python classroom/crew.py --offline

SCOUT: available options from MCP
PLANNER: 2 x Veg sandwich
TOTAL: Rs 120 within Rs 150
bottom: Actual CrewAI tasks; --offline uses scripted brains.
say: Read the SCRIPTED label if using offline. The actual CrewAI orchestration, MCP lookup and task context run. A live Gemini run requires separate private rehearsal. Do not call this a benchmark or autonomous AI when scripted.
do: Run & $py classroom/crew.py --offline. Point to SCOUT HANDOFF then PLANNER.
fallback: Use saved_runs/crew.txt; do not install CrewAI during class.

title: When does a team earn its cost?
bottom: An orchestrator assigns work; a sequence has a fixed handoff.
say: Briefly sketch a coordinator choosing a menu or facilities specialist. That is a different optional pattern from the sequential crew we ran. Keep its implementation for later.
ask: What would two lunch agents add besides latency?

title: Choose for the job
rows: LangGraph workflow with agents where useful
Consider a CrewAI team and its cost
bottom: These are starting points, not exclusive framework capabilities.
say: Give three quick scenarios: one menu question, an action needing approval, and research followed by writing. Students choose and give one reason. CrewAI also has flows; LangGraph can host multiple agents.
ask: Which is the simplest design that meets each requirement?

title: MCP and A2A connect different things
bottom: Two agents do not automatically implement the A2A protocol.
say: Spend at most one minute on A2A and the remaining minute recapping categories. ReAct and handoffs are patterns; LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI are frameworks; MCP/A2A are protocols.
do: Skip this teaser if behind; do not introduce protocol messages or another server.

title: Give the files clear jobs
code:
README.md          what it does and how to run
AGENTS.md          supported coding instructions
data/menu.json     fictional records
menu_tools.py      ordinary functions
my_agent.py        model + tools + loop
bottom: Instruction filename support depends on your coding client.
say: Now that the program works, the folders have a purpose. Show the small project. Mention CLAUDE.md/GEMINI.md as other client conventions. Arbitrary Markdown is not automatically loaded or enforced.
ask: Where should a price change live? Where should a run command live?

title: Write a useful project instruction
code:
# Canteen project rules

- Use data/menu.json for menu facts.
- Explain a proposed change before editing.
- Run the changed behavior and report the result.
- Keep API keys out of source and commits.
bottom: A heading and clear bullets are enough to start.
say: Write these together, then ask each student for one useful instruction in a note or supported project file. Explain the difference between guidance and runtime enforcement.
do: Use a plain Markdown file or paper if the coding client is unavailable. This is a two-minute introduction; the longer documentation lab is after class.

title: Keep control of allowed actions
code:
if call["name"] not in allowed_tools:
    raise ValueError("Tool is not allowed")

# Also bound the number of model steps.
# Validate arguments before execution.
# Keep private configuration off screen.
bottom: Prompts guide behavior. Code enforces boundaries.
say: Use one narrow safety example after the agent makes sense. A model request cannot execute an unregistered function through our loop. Avoid a new long threat-model lecture.
do: Open classroom/manual_loop.py and show the allowed lookup and step limit. Run classroom/safety_demo.py for a deliberately injected forbidden request. Label it as injected.
ask: Would writing "be safe" in a prompt replace this check?
fallback: Read the seven-line boundary example and the expected refusal.

title: Review one small AI-assisted change
rows: Read the new function and registration.
Ask a question that needs the tool.
bottom: Ask what changed, why it works and what actually ran.
say: One minute. An AI coding editor is optional. The skill is making a small understandable change and observing its behavior, not accepting a whole generated project. Keep the long fake-wrap review after class.

title: What will you build next?
quote:
One new tool
One graph route
Or compare one agent with a team
bottom: Questions · repository and exercises in your student kit
say: Reserve the last ten minutes for questions. Invite a short explanation of one tool call or framework choice. Direct students to classroom/README.md and docs/LEARNING_PATH.md. The repository stays private until explicitly released; distribute the ZIP through the organiser.
do: Close at 13:00. Do not add a surprise final installation or advanced topic.
ask: What can your agent now do that it could not do at the beginning?
